01 — Why it matters

A worn or mismatched nozzle quietly decides your yield

Nobody orders a mounter because of its nozzles — but the nozzle is the only thing that actually touches your component. Its tip geometry sets whether a 0402 lifts square or skews; its bore and vacuum path set whether a part sticks or drops; its material sets how fast it wears. On a high-mix EMS line, the nozzle is where pick errors, tombstoning and 'mystery' reject spikes really come from. Southern Machinery makes the nozzle the predictable part.

01

The tip sets the pick

A mounter does not pick a component; it picks a position through a tip. When the tip is wrong for the part — too wide, too narrow, the wrong material — the head reaches, misses the centre of gravity, and the placement is marginal. Every mispick traces back to a tip that was never matched to the part.

02

Wear is silent until it is a reject

Ceramic and metal tips drift by microns as they wear; rubber tips harden and lose grip. Nothing alarms when this happens — the reject rate simply climbs and the operator blames the feeder, the tape, the program. By the time it is noticed, dozens of boards have been reworked or scrapped.

03

OEM pricing squeezes the spares budget

Genuine nozzles are expensive and often carry long lead times, so factories run them past their useful life to avoid a stop. That is a false economy: one stopped head costs more in an hour than a whole set of matched nozzles. A traceable aftermarket source turns the spares line from a hostage into a plan.

02 — The method

From your head to a fitted nozzle in six documented moves

Nozzle supply is not catalogue roulette. It is a matching discipline: read the machine, cross-reference the part number, choose the geometry and material for the actual component, then verify dimensions before it ever reaches your line. This is the sequence Southern Machinery engineers follow on every Yamaha order, and it is the same one we invite you to run against your own part master.

01

Read the mounter and head

Everything starts with the machine model and head — YS12, YS24, YSM, YG100, YG200, YG300, YV88, YV100, YV112, YT16 or MG. The head fixes the shank, the holder interface and the vacuum take-off, so it is the first fact we record.

02

Cross-reference the part number

We match your nozzle against the Yamaha Mounter Nozzle List and the supplier document — the KM0, KV6, KV7, KV8, KGS, KGT, KGR, KHN, KHY, KLF and LC/LG dispenser series — so the replacement carries the same identity your program expects.

03

Choose the tip geometry

The component decides the tip: a 0402 needs a fine single-bore tip, a QFP or large electrolytic needs a wide or multi-bore gripper, an odd-form part may need a V-shape, narrow-pitch, reflector or Y-shape (王) profile. The bore is stated as inner/outer diameter — Φ0.4/Φ0.7 up to Φ6.0/Φ4.5.

04

Select material and coating

Ceramic for fine-pitch, low-static, long-life picking; tungsten or spring steel for rugged larger parts; rubber or silicone for sensitive bodies; metal with O-ring where a mechanical gripper must close on a lead or terminal. Material is a wear-and-grip decision, not a default.

05

Manufacture and dimensionally verify

Each nozzle is ground to the OEM dimensions and checked — tip diameter, bore, concentricity, shank fit — before it ships. The document records single/double action (1D/1S, 2D/2S) and pitch values (P=0.8 to 2.0 mm); those are the numbers we hold to.

06

Drop in and confirm the first pick

Because the fit is dimensional to the head holder, the nozzle drops in without re-tramming. We ask for a first-article pick on your own tape so the match is proven on your line, not just on the drawing.

Mounter families, P/N series, tip specifications, materials and component sizes are quoted from the Southern Machinery SMT Nozzle Supplier document (Yamaha pages) and the YAMAHA Mounter Nozzle List.

How the nozzle is built to pick

Ceramic fine-pitch tips

Low static, hard and wear-resistant — the choice for 0402, 0603 and 1005 chips where the pick centre must not drift.

Tungsten & spring-steel tips

Rugged metal tips for larger chips, MELF and IC bodies that would chip a softer material.

Rubber & silicone tips

Gentle grip on sensitive or irregular bodies; the supplier document lists rubber tips for large components and MELF.

Metal + O-ring grippers

Mechanical closing tips for terminals, connectors and odd-form parts that vacuum alone cannot hold.

Ground concentricity

The tip is ground to the OEM dimensions so the pick position stays the same on cycle one and cycle five hundred thousand.

Clean vacuum channel

Bore and channel integrity keep suction stable and resist the clogging that turns into intermittent mispicks.

The four nozzle families we make

Vacuum nozzles

The everyday pick tip — single and double bore, ceramic to metal, for chips, MELF, IC and QFP on YS/YSM/YG/YV heads.

Gripper nozzles

Mechanical closing tips for terminals, connectors and odd-form parts, including mini-chuck and E-cap variants.

Dispenser nozzles

LC1 / LC6 / LG0 series for HSD and Yamaha dispensing heads — adhesive, flux and solder-paste application tips.

Custom odd-form nozzles

V-shape, narrow-pitch, reflector and bespoke geometries designed from a photograph when no catalog tip fits.

ARTICLE 01The one millimetre nobody specs — and why it decides your yield

The nozzle is the only thing in the pick-and-place cycle that touches the component, yet it rarely appears on the machine spec sheet.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

Every SMT engineer can name the machine that placed a part. Almost none can name the nozzle that picked it. That is the gap: the nozzle is the single component in the whole pick-and-place cycle that physically touches your board, and it is the one nobody specs.

Think about the last 'mystery' reject spike you chased. You looked at the program, the feeder, the tape, the calibration. You probably did not look at the tip — because it looked fine, and because it never occurred to you that a few microns of tip wear could move the pick centre off the component's centre of gravity. That is exactly what it does. The head reaches for a position; the tip decides whether the part actually sits where the head expects.

The reusable method is to treat the nozzle as a spec'd part of the process, not a consumable you replace when it visibly breaks. Three questions on your changeover card: what is the tip size and material for this part, what is the bore and vacuum path, and how many cycles has this tip run? If you cannot answer all three, you are running a component you have not specified.

Southern Machinery's Yamaha nozzle range is built around that discipline: a documented tip window from the 0402 micro-chip (0.25 × 0.35 mm) up to the large-component nozzle (Φ15.0 mm), across ceramic, tungsten, spring steel, rubber and metal-O-ring materials, mapped to the mounter families you actually run — YS12, YS24, YSM, YG100, YG200, YG300, YV88, YV100, YV112, YT16 and MG. The tip is the product; the rest is the head.

Once the nozzle is on the card, the second-order effect shows up over a quarter: the pick centre stops drifting, the reject rate stops having a personality, and the conversation with the operator changes from 'what did you touch' to 'when do we swap'. The parts stay the same. The behaviour of the line changes.

Send us your machine model, head position and the part number printed on the nozzle — or just a clear photo of the tip. We will match it against the Yamaha Mounter Nozzle List and tell you, honestly, whether a standard tip fixes your problem or whether you need a custom geometry. info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576.

ARTICLE 02Why mispicks trace back to a tip, not a program

A repeatable method for separating a nozzle problem from a feeder or program problem before you change anything.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

When a board rejects, the first instinct is to blame the program or the feeder. Both are usually innocent. The mispick you are staring at is far more likely to be a tip that was never matched to the part it was asked to hold.

Here is the honest diagnosis most vendors skip: a mounter does not pick a component, it picks a position through a tip. If the tip is too wide for a 0402, it scoops two pads' worth of air and the part skews. If the bore is too narrow for a MELF, the vacuum never fully breaks and the part hangs on. If the material is wrong, the tip either grips too hard and marks the body or too softly and drops it. None of these are program bugs. They are geometry.

The reusable method is to separate the three suspects before you change anything. Freeze the program and the feeder, then run the same part on a known-good nozzle of the correct series. If the mispick follows the nozzle, it was the tip. If it follows the position on the bank, it was the feeder. If it follows the coordinates, only then look at the program. Ten minutes of isolation beats a week of blaming.

For the nozzle side, the matching is documented: the Southern Machinery SMT Nozzle Supplier list maps each Yamaha mounter family to its nozzle series — KM0, KV6, KV7, KV8, KGS, KGT, KGR, KHN, KHY, KLF for placement, LC1, LC6 and LG0 for dispensing — with tip size, bore (inner/outer diameter from Φ0.4/Φ0.7 up to Φ6.0/Φ4.5), action (1D/1S, 2D/2S) and material stated. The right tip is a lookup, not a guess.

Log the swap on the changeover card with the part number and the cycle count. The next time the same part mispicks, you start from evidence instead of from blame, and the isolation test takes two minutes instead of two hours.

Send us the part that is mispicking and the nozzle you think is on the head. We will tell you which series and tip it should be, and ship a matched sample so you can run the isolation test on your own line.

ARTICLE 03Ceramic, tungsten or rubber — choosing the tip material

Material is a wear-and-grip decision. Here is how to read your parts and pick the right one.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

'Ceramic, metal or rubber?' sounds like a shopping question. It is actually an engineering one, and getting it wrong is why a tip either wears out in a week or marks the component you were trying to protect.

The method is to read two things about the part before you pick a material: its body and its weight, and the pick force your head applies. A 0402 or 0603 chip is tiny, light and static-prone — ceramic wins because it is hard, resists wear, and sheds the part cleanly when the vacuum breaks. A large electrolytic or a heavy IC wants a metal tip — tungsten or spring steel — because a ceramic edge on a big bore would chip. A sensitive or irregular body wants rubber or silicone, which grips softly and conforms. A terminal or connector that vacuum cannot hold wants a mechanical gripper, metal with an O-ring that closes on the lead.

The Southern Machinery document lists all four materials against real Yamaha part numbers, so this is not theory — the ceramic tips run the fine-pitch chips, the metal and O-ring tips run the larger IC and SOP/QFP bodies, the rubber tips run the large components and MELF. Each material is a wear-and-grip trade-off, and the table shows which trade-off was made for which part.

Once you choose by the part rather than by habit, the failure modes stop surprising you. Ceramic will not mark a chip; metal will not chip on a heavy part; rubber will not crush a sensitive body; the gripper will not drop a terminal. The tip becomes the predictable variable instead of the recurring mystery.

Add the material to your part master next to the tip size, and review it whenever a new component family arrives. A part that used to be picked by a generic ceramic tip may want a rubber or gripper nozzle, and the time to notice is before the first shift, not after the first reject.

Tell us what you place — the component, its body and its weight — and the head you place it on. We will recommend the material and ship samples of the two or three tips worth testing, with the reasoning written down.

ARTICLE 04The part number you cannot read

How to identify a worn Yamaha nozzle and turn an illegible marking into an exact replacement.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

Half the nozzle orders we get start with a photo of a part number that has worn off. The laser marking is tiny, it sits on a curved ceramic body, and after a few hundred thousand picks it is simply gone. The factory knows it has a KV8 or a KLF on the head; it cannot read which one.

The method for turning an illegible nozzle into an exact replacement is three facts and one picture. Fact one: the mounter model — YS12, YS24, YSM, YG100, YG200, YG300, YV88, YV100, YV112, YT16 or MG. Fact two: the head position and whether it is a placement or a dispenser head. Fact three: the component you place there. The picture: the tip, straight on and from the side, next to a coin for scale. With those, the Yamaha Mounter Nozzle List does the rest — the model and head narrow the series, the component narrows the tip, and the photo confirms the geometry.

This is why Southern Machinery keeps the full compatibility mapping rather than a price list. The document records the P/N series by machine — KV8-M77xx for YSM40 and YV100X, KGS and KV7-M77xx for YG200 and YG300, KGT for YG100R, KHN and KHY for YS12/YS100 and YG12/YG300, KLF for YS12/YS24, and the LC1/LC6/LG0 N-, M- and P-coded tips for dispensing — so an unreadable marking becomes a lookup on the machine, not on the ink.

Once identified, the replacement carries the same identity your program expects: same series prefix, same bore, same material, dimensionally matched to the holder. The part number you could not read is now a named line on your spares shelf, and the next swap does not start with a photo shoot.

Put a small label of the machine model and head position on your spares register, not just the P/N — because the P/N is the thing that wears off and the model is the thing that does not.

Send us the photo and the three facts. We will identify the series, confirm the tip against the component, and quote a matched replacement with a one-day spare-parts lead time on the standard family.

ARTICLE 05Running a nozzle past its life is a false economy

The real cost of stretching a tip, measured against the hour of head time it eventually costs you.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

The most expensive nozzle is the one you keep too long. Running a tip past its life saves a purchase order and costs you an hour of head time — usually at the worst possible moment.

The arithmetic is simple and most factories refuse to do it. A high-speed Yamaha head is a six-figure-per-hour asset. A worn nozzle does not announce itself; it shows up as a rising reject rate, a skewed part that passes inspection and fails at wave solder, and the occasional stopped head mid-shift. One stopped head for an hour costs more than a full set of matched nozzles for the machine. Stretching the spares budget to avoid a small purchase is a false economy that hides inside the 'consumables' line.

The method is to swap on evidence, not on failure. Track the cycle count per tip, clean the vacuum channel on a schedule, and set a swap interval from the wear you actually see — the reject rate, not the calendar. Pair the nozzles with an automatic cleaner (the S-6200 or SCM24) to recover suction between swaps, and keep named-part-number spares on the shelf so a scheduled swap is a morning's work.

This is exactly what the one-day spare-parts lead time and the single-piece-to-batch MOQ are for. You do not need to hoard nozzles to avoid running a worn tip; you need a traceable source that ships the right part number fast, and a cleaning program that stretches the useful life honestly. Both are in the document, not in a promise.

Put the swap interval and the cleaner on the maintenance plan next to the nozzle part number. The tip that fails silently is the one you never scheduled — so schedule it.

Want the shelf inventory? Send us your head count and daily volumes. We will turn the named part numbers into a spares kit with quantities and a cleaning plan, and quote it with the nozzles.

ARTICLE 06Odd-form parts need odd-form tips

V-shape, narrow-pitch, reflector and gripper nozzles — matching geometry to the parts that defeat a standard tip.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

Ask an operator which parts are hardest to place and they will not say the BGA. They will say the terminal, the connector, the odd-shaped thing that a standard vacuum tip keeps dropping or skewing.

Odd-form parts defeat a round tip for a physical reason: there is no flat, clean surface for vacuum to grab, or the part must be held by a lead or a body that a suction cup cannot seat on. The answer is geometry, not force. A V-shape tip cradles a cylindrical body. A narrow-pitch tip reaches a fine-pitch IC without disturbing its neighbours. A reflector tip handles the transparent or reflective parts that confuse the sensor. A mechanical gripper — metal with an O-ring that closes — grabs a terminal or connector by the lead when vacuum cannot hold it at all.

The Southern Machinery document lists these geometries against real Yamaha part numbers, so odd-form picking is a documented path, not an experiment: V-shape and narrow-pitch variants appear across the KV8 and KGS series, Y-shape (王) and octagon/rectangle tips appear for specific IC and MELF bodies, and the gripper and mini-chuck nozzles cover terminals and E-cap-class parts. Each is a shape chosen for a shape.

Once you match geometry to the part, the awkward ones stop being the line's weak point. The terminal that used to drop is held by a gripper; the fine-pitch IC that used to disturb its neighbour is reached by a narrow-pitch tip; the transparent part that confused the sensor is picked by a reflector. The part did not change. The tip did.

Keep a small set of the odd-form geometries on the shelf with the parts they belong to, and flag them on the changeover card so the next engineer reaches for the right shape instead of the generic one.

Have a part that keeps dropping or skewing? Send a photo of the component and the board. We will tell you whether a V-shape, narrow-pitch, reflector or gripper tip is the answer, and what it costs.

ARTICLE 07You do not need a drawing to get a custom nozzle

The three photographs and two numbers that start a five-day nozzle design.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

The scariest sentence in nozzle supply is 'our part is special, there is no tip for it'. The least scary version of it is a photograph.

Every custom project stalls at the same place: the customer is asked for a drawing and does not have one — because the part is a locally-sourced connector, a custom terminal, a component with no CAD. The truth our engineering desk has learned over fifteen years of spare parts: a custom nozzle design does not need a drawing. It needs to see the part, and to know how many you place.

Here is the three-photo method. Photo one: the component out of the package, next to a coin — that gives us the body and the tip size, from the 0402 micro-chip up to the Φ15.0 mm large-component nozzle, or tells us it is outside the window. Photo two: the part from the side and from the pick face, so we can see whether it needs a bore, a V-shape, a narrow-pitch or a gripper that closes on a lead. Photo three: the board, so we can see spacing and neighbours and know whether a reflector or a Y-shape (王) profile is needed. Then two numbers: the machine model and your daily volume.

With five inputs, the documented five-day design service returns a nozzle concept — geometry, bore (inner/outer diameter), material, and the shank interface to your head — not a brochure. The custom odd-form path is the documented path across the whole range: the same document that lists the standard Yamaha series is the one we extend when no catalog tip fits.

Design cycles shrink when the evidence arrives early. The project that starts with three photos finishes with a first-article pick on your own tape; the project that starts with a request for a drawing finishes in a shared drive.

Take the three photos today and send them to info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576. We will tell you within one working day whether your special part is a catalog tip or a five-day custom design — and what each one costs.

ARTICLE 08A nozzle budget you can actually defend

Four honest lines that turn spares from a grudge purchase into a plan.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

Most nozzle quotations are dishonest in the same direction: the vendor's sheet shows a saving you will never collect. Here is the opposite method — four lines, your numbers, and a bias toward under-claiming.

Line one: how many nozzles do you actually replace in a year, and what do you pay for each today? Not the brochure figure — the invoices. Line two: what would a matched aftermarket nozzle cost, and what share of that spend could you realistically switch? Be honest; some heads you will keep genuine. Line three: what does an hour of stopped head time cost you, and how many changeover hours and working days does a good nozzle source save you per year? Line four: add the purchase saving to the downtime you avoid. That total is your real number, and every figure in it is one you typed.

The calculator on this page runs exactly those four lines, with nothing pre-baked. No invented time studies, no competitor-bashing multipliers, no price hard-coded anywhere — the OEM price and our price are both boxes you fill in. The defaults are placeholders for the arithmetic, not claims about your factory.

Now the savings the method deliberately leaves out, because they are yours to prove: the tombstoned and skewed parts a worn tip lets through, the rework and scrap those cause, and the reject spikes a drifting nozzle hides until they arrive at wave solder. Those are real, and they are bigger than the purchase price — but we will not put a fake number on them.

Every factory that starts measuring nozzle spend finds it was hiding in someone else's cost line — usually 'consumables' or 'overtime'. The four lines make it visible, and visible is negotiable.

Send us the four numbers — or just your machine model, head count and current nozzle invoices. We will turn them into a matched nozzle plan with named part numbers, a one-day spare-parts lead time on the standard family, and a quotation that matches the arithmetic you already trust.

FAQ

Questions EMS buyers ask before ordering

Do these fit genuine Yamaha heads?
Yes. We match the shank and holder interface dimensionally to the OEM nozzle for the mounter family you run — YS12, YS24, YSM, YG100, YG200, YG300, YV88, YV100, YV112, YT16 and MG — so the nozzle drops into the head without re-tramming. Send the exact part number and we confirm the fit before you order.
What is the minimum order and lead time?
We supply from a single replacement piece to a full production batch. The standard nozzle family carries a documented one-day spare-parts lead time; custom or odd-form tips follow the quoted schedule after the design step.
Can you make a nozzle that is not in the list?
Yes. The documented five-day design service starts from a photograph, not a drawing. Send the part, a handful of them, and the board, plus your daily volume, and we return a nozzle concept — geometry, bore, material and head interface.
Ceramic, metal or rubber — which should I choose?
It depends on the component and your wear pattern. Ceramic suits fine-pitch 0402/0603/1005 with low static and long life; metal (tungsten / spring steel) suits larger, tougher parts; rubber and metal-O-ring suit sensitive bodies and mechanical grippers. Tell us what you place and we will recommend.
How do I find my nozzle part number?
The P/N is usually laser-marked on the nozzle body (for example a KV8-M77xx or KLF-M77xx prefix) or listed in your spares register. If it is worn off, a clear photo of the tip and the machine model is enough for us to cross-reference the Yamaha Mounter Nozzle List.
Do you supply nozzles for other mounters?
Yes. The same document covers ASM / Siemens, JUKI, FUJI NXT, Panasonic NPM and Hitachi nozzles, plus fully customised gripper and vacuum tips. Ask about the brands your line runs.
How do I get more life out of a nozzle?
Keep the vacuum channel clean and track cycle counts. Pair the nozzles with an S-6200 or SCM24 automatic nozzle cleaner to recover suction, and swap on a schedule from a named part number rather than waiting for a reject spike.
How do I get a quote?
Email info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576 with the machine model, head position and nozzle part number (or a photo). We reply with a matched part, price and lead time, usually the same working day.
